title: UK and EU Agree to Link Emissions Trading Schemes — Ship & Bunker
summary: The UK and EU Emissions Trading Schemes will link from January 1, 2028, with the UK scheme belatedly expanding to cover 50% of international voyage emissions, merely aligning with the EU's established scope. This integration, alongside the UK scrapping its auction reserve price, risks weakening the financial incentive for prompt decarbonization, given UK allowances' historical discount to EUAs. Specific derogations for island ro-pax and ice-class vessels until 2030 further highlight persistent loopholes, allowing certain fleets to delay meaningful emissions reductions.
content:
Link intended to be operational from January 1, 2028, with UK and EU allowances valid in either scheme

UK ETS to cover 50% of international voyage emissions from the same date

UK auction reserve price scrapped when the link goes live

Northern Ireland derogation goes, island ro-pax and ice-class derogations kept to end-2030

The UK and EU have agreed to link their emissions trading systems, with the link intended to be operational from January 1, 2028, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said in an explainer published on Friday.

From that date allowances issued under either scheme can be used for compliance in the other, including for 2027 emissions, with the first joint surrender deadline on September 30, 2028.

Operators should also be able to use one pool of allowances for both their UK and EU obligations, without needing to buy UK allowances (UKAs) and EU allowances (EUAs) separately, greatly simplifying compliance requirements for those on international voyages.

For shipping, the agreement confirms that the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) will expand to cover 50% of emissions from international voyages by ships of 5,000 GT and above from the same date, alongside the 100% of domestic and in-port emissions it has covered since July 1, 2026.

The expansion was first set out last November with the same January 1, 2028 start, so the UK's coverage of international shipping and the allowance link now begin together.

The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) already covers 50% of emissions on voyages between an EU port and a port outside the bloc.

As part of the move, the UK will remove its auction reserve price when the link goes live, since "it would not be practical or desirable to maintain a price floor in only one part of a linked market," the explainer says.

UK allowances have traded below EUAs since the scheme began, and earlier this year Ship & Bunker calculated an average discount of 21.8% in the first half of 2026.

Derogations

The agreement removes the temporary 50% surrender derogation for voyages between Northern Ireland and Great Britain, "as planned", so that all covered Irish Sea voyages face the same 100% obligation.

The UK will align with the EU's temporary derogation for passenger and ro-pax voyages to islands with fewer than 200,000 people and no road or rail link to the mainland, until at least December 31, 2030, and ice-class ships will get a 5% surrender derogation to the same date.

Shipping companies will be able to apply a zero emission factor to biofuels, RFNBOs and recycled carbon fuels that meet the Renewable Energy Directive's criteria.

Should a global measure be adopted at the IMO, the UK "will review its interactions with our own policy, to avoid any double charging of emissions", the document says.

That said, the IBIA Annual Convention in New York heard last week that the EU is unlikely to give up the ETS whatever the outcome on the IMO Net-Zero Framework, with Peter Keller, Chairman of SEA-LNG, saying: "What government do we know anywhere in the world is prepared to give up tax revenue?"

The deal came a day after the UK Chamber of Shipping called on both sides to use the reset talks to cut costs, asking for ETS revenues to support shipping's decarbonisation and for a full economic impact assessment before the UK ETS was extended internationally.

"We also need to see the revenues raised from shipping support shipping's decarbonisation, rather than simply increasing ETS and compliance costs without delivering additional emissions reductions," a Chamber spokesperson said in a statement on Thursday.

The explainer makes no mention of revenue for maritime decarbonisation.
